articles.text: How long would it take you to run three miles through Piedmont? For Walter Teitelbaum, a 21-year-old Piedmont High alum and cross-country runner, it only took 16 minutes. Teitelbaum was declared the overall winner of the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, finishing ahead of more than 2,200 runners and nearly one minute faster than the 2nd and 3rd place runners. While waiting for the start of the Thanksgiving morning 8:30 a.m. 5-kilometer race, runners and onlookers were treated to a half dozen fanfares by seven symphony musicians playing bona fide Belgian and French hunting horns. It was an appropriate announcement of one of the city’s largest public events of the year. Runners stretched out on Highland Avenue in front of the Exedra in a line a half-block long. The route was the same as in previous years, winding its way along Highland, Wildwood, and La Salle Avenues, crawling up the incline on Sea View before dashing down Mountain Avenue and onto Craig and Vista to the finish line. In addition to competitive runners and recreational runners, there was an abundance of families with strollers, including multiple race winner Crosby Freeman, running with his wife Jessica while pushing a stroller with 10-week old Spencer Freeman. And there were plenty of people sipping cocoa and coffee while giving their dogs a little morning workout.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8, at 5 p.m. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont Turkey Trot organizers thank all the runners, walkers, cheering families and friends, volunteers and sponsors for making the 20th annual Piedmont Turkey Trot a success. Welcomed clear skies greeted the more than 2,000 runners and walkers in the race this year. It is a matter of great pride to see Piedmont bringing friends and families of multiple generations from all over the country to participate in this Thanksgiving Day community tradition. Coordinating a race of this size takes many hands and the organizers are incredibly grateful to have the support and unwavering commitment of the City of Piedmont, the Piedmont Public Works Department, the Piedmont Police Department, and the Piedmont Fire Department. The excellent work of a large and energetic group of volunteers working on Wednesday and on Race Day made everything seem effortless. Their spirit of service and dedication to the community and the Piedmont Turkey Trot is greatly appreciated. Many thanks to the sponsors: Transports, Village Market, Corcoran Global Living, Piedmont Grocery, MB Jessee Painting, J. Miller Flowers, Dr. Frank Helm, Dr. Gregory Young, Ken Betts Company, OCHO Candy and Piedmont Post. The event simply could not happen without their strong support. And finally, thank you to the entire Piedmont community for sharing this day and for graciously accommodating the 2,000+ race participants and volunteers as they wound through the streets of this beautiful community. We appreciate your continued support of the Piedmont Turkey Trot and we look forward to seeing everyone next year. –Race Organizers Debra Dryden Jeanine Holmlund Sydney Proctor Chris Smith Marilyn Weber Lesley Zalewski
articles.title: Thanks to many for success of the 20th Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot

articles.text: Many people are seeking COVID-19 testing after the Thanksgiving holiday and as the threat of a new variant emerges. The Curative mobile COVID- 19 testing clinic at Piedmont City Hall administered 44 PCR tests on Sunday, November 28. By noon the next day, November 29, Curative had administered more than 40 tests. “In total, since we launched in Piedmont on November 7, we have administered 349 tests,” confirmed Curative Regional Partners Manager Shoshana Gould. “With increased travel and exposure due to the holidays coupled with concern about the Omicron variant, we are seeing an increased number of tests administered.” Air and auto travel was expected to double this year and return to near-pre-pandemic levels. “For Thanksgiving 2021, between Friday, November 19th and Sunday, November 28th, over 148,000 passengers departed from Oakland International Airport. This is over 2.5 times the number of passengers that departed OAK during Thanksgiving 2020,” said Kaley Skantz, Airport Spokesperson for Oakland International. The U.S Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screened over two million airline passengers on Sunday, November 28, the highest number of daily passengers since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. To ease travel safety concerns, many international airports are offering rapid COVID testing. COVID testing is available at Oakland International Airport for travelers with appointments made in advance. Federal law and county order require that masks are properly worn over your nose For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. and mouth in all areas within Oakland International Airport, with few exceptions. The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) strongly recommends COVID vaccine boosters for all adults as cases are expected to rise this winter, regardless of travel plans. “We expect a rise in COVID-19 cases as people gather with friends and family indoors and travel for the holidays,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Health Officer. “If you are a fully vaccinated adult and enough time has passed since your vaccination, get your booster as soon as you can.” Health care systems, pharmacies, and community-based clinics are offering boosters and a person can receive their booster from any location, not necessarily the same location where they received their initial vaccine series, according to ACPHD. Any eligible person seeking a booster dose should contact their health care provider or access a booster through a retail pharmacy, like CVS Pharmacy or Walgreens. Booster appointments are also available through MyTurn.ca.gov.

articles.text: Firefighter/paramedic Todd Gerard will officially retire from the Piedmont Fire Department on Sunday, December 5 after 28 years of service. He joined the department in 1993 and brought with him years of experience as a trained paramedic. “Todd Gerard has been a steady, calm fixture in Piedmont for nearly three decades,” noted Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “His skills, experience, and easy-going nature will be sorely missed.” Gerard grew up in Huntington Beach in Southern California. He came north to attend American River College in Sacramento where he obtained his degree in Fire Science. “After I completed school, I realized I’m not a hot weather person, so I moved to the Bay Area to look for work,” he said. Gerard started working with a local ambulance company in 1987, becoming a field supervisor for Acme Western Ambulance Services in the East Bay until 1991. He received his paramedic training at Chabot College in Hayward, and then signed on as an Alameda County Paramedic in 1992. A claim to fame is that he served as an on-site paramedic for the TV show Nash Bridges. “I worked on movie sets for about three years part-time. It was fun, but the hours were long – all night, all day,” Gerard said. “I worked on sets when I started working in Piedmont.” Nearly 35 years of paramedic service earns Gerard a well-deserved retirement, to which he modestly replied, “It’s just what I do. After all these years. I love being a paramedic.” His extensive background in paramedic services earned him a position with the Piedmont Fire Department in 1993. He was hired full-time after a year of working each shift in the Department part-time. In the last 10 years, Gerard noted that Piedmont Fire crews have been helping with wildfires more often and throughout the state – from Napa County to Santa Barbara. One of the most devastating fires during his time with the department, the 2017 Thomas Fire, had Piedmont crews stationed in Southern California for two weeks. Piedmont crews were assigned to tactical and structural Piedmont Paramedic-firefighter Todd Gerard. protection, working round-theclock, 24 hours on and 24 hours off. At the time, the fire was the third-largest in state history. Gerard was sent to assist with a second crew of Piedmont firefighters and paramedics, along with Capt. Jon Fitzpatrick, engineer Russ San Filippo, and firefighter/paramedic Zach Heliker. “Each year since then, the fires have gotten bigger and bigger,” Gerard said. Last year, Northern California experienced the most destructive wildfires on record, and Piedmont crews were there to assist. Gerard’s focus as a paramedic was an integral part of the crew; ready to administer medications, provide advanced life support, and perform CPR. Gerard gave credit to his crew members. “My focus [as a paramedic] was not actually fighting the fires or carrying [the lines]. I’m almost 60, so I let the younger guys handle that,” he said with a smile. Firefighter/paramedic Brian Gidney, who has worked with Gerard since 2005, described him as an ideal firefighter. “Todd retiring is very exciting and a well-deserved end of his career. But to not have him around will be hard to adjust to,” Gidney said. “To describe Todd is akin to describing much of an ideal firefighter. He is calm in a way that reassures everyone around him; he cares for others truly like they were his own family; and he is driven is to be a helper and problem solver. “Above all, Todd is one of the most humble people I’ve ever known. Personally and professionally, he has been an example to live up to – and I know I’m not the only one who feels that way.” Gerard said he is looking forward to retirement so he can devote time to his passion for skiing, a sport he has done nearly his entire life. He acknowledged that he will really miss the department. “It has been my family for all these years,” he noted. He observed that they will miss him, too, but said they may miss his famous oatmeal-l banana pancakes even more. Gerard will retire in Reno, Nevada, where he intends to continue in public service as a volunteer with the Red Cross or another non-profit organization. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont residents who have missed the first two community workshops on the planned community pool and would like to add additional comments may complete an online survey prior to the next workshop on December 14. On November 16, The City of Piedmont and ELS Architecture and Urban Design co-hosted the second workshop of a three-part series to develop the design of the new Piedmont Community Pool. Nearly 100 people participated in the second workshop at Veterans Hall; coupled with responses from surveys, the total number of responses received comes from at least 300 community members. Workshop two culminated in the overwhelming selection of “Concept C.” To add comments before the next workshop, visit https://www. surveymonkey.com/r/piedmontcommunitypoolworkshop2. By following the link, you can view and add comments and questions for all three concepts presented by ELS.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 1, 2021 3 Todd Gerard to retire from Fire Dept. December 5 By Allyson Aleksey Firefighter/paramedic Todd Gerard will officially retire from the Piedmont Fire Department on Sunday, December 5 after 28 years of service. He joined the department in 1993 and brought with him years of experience as a trained paramedic. “Todd Gerard has been a steady, calm fixture in Piedmont for nearly three decades,” noted Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “His skills, experience, and easy-going nature will be sorely missed.” Gerard grew up in Huntington Beach in Southern California. He came north to attend American River College in Sacramento where he obtained his degree in Fire Science. “After I completed school, I realized I’m not a hot weather person, so I moved to the Bay Area to look for work,” he said. Gerard started working with a local ambulance company in 1987, becoming a field supervisor for Acme Western Ambulance Services in the East Bay until 1991. He received his paramedic training at Chabot College in Hayward, and then signed on as an Alameda County Paramedic in 1992. A claim to fame is that he served as an on-site paramedic for the TV show Nash Bridges. “I worked on movie sets for about three years part-time. It was fun, but the hours were long – all night, all day,” Gerard said. “I worked on sets when I started working in Piedmont.” Nearly 35 years of paramedic service earns Gerard a well-deserved retirement, to which he modestly replied, “It’s just what I do. After all these years. I love being a paramedic.” His extensive background in paramedic services earned him a position with the Piedmont Fire Department in 1993. He was hired full-time after a year of working each shift in the Department part-time. In the last 10 years, Gerard noted that Piedmont Fire crews have been helping with wildfires more often and throughout the state – from Napa County to Santa Barbara. One of the most devastating fires during his time with the department, the 2017 Thomas Fire, had Piedmont crews stationed in Southern California for two weeks. Piedmont crews were assigned to tactical and structural Piedmont Paramedic-firefighter Todd Gerard. protection, working round-theclock, 24 hours on and 24 hours off. At the time, the fire was the third-largest in state history. Gerard was sent to assist with a second crew of Piedmont firefighters and paramedics, along with Capt. Jon Fitzpatrick, engineer Russ San Filippo, and firefighter/paramedic Zach Heliker. “Each year since then, the fires have gotten bigger and bigger,” Gerard said. Last year, Northern California experienced the most destructive wildfires on record, and Piedmont crews were there to assist. Gerard’s focus as a paramedic was an integral part of the crew; ready to administer medications, provide advanced life support, and perform CPR. Gerard gave credit to his crew members. “My focus [as a paramedic] was not actually fighting the fires or carrying [the lines]. I’m almost 60, so I let the younger guys handle that,” he said with a smile. Firefighter/paramedic Brian Gidney, who has worked with Gerard since 2005, described him as an ideal firefighter. “Todd retiring is very exciting and a well-deserved end of his career. But to not have him around will be hard to adjust to,” Gidney said. “To describe Todd is akin to describing much of an ideal firefighter. He is calm in a way that reassures everyone around him; he cares for others truly like they were his own family; and he is driven is to be a helper and problem solver. “Above all, Todd is one of the most humble people I’ve ever known. Personally and professionally, he has been an example to live up to – and I know I’m not the only one who feels that way.” Gerard said he is looking forward to retirement so he can devote time to his passion for skiing, a sport he has done nearly his entire life. He acknowledged that he will really miss the department. “It has been my family for all these years,” he noted. He observed that they will miss him, too, but said they may miss his famous oatmeal-l banana pancakes even more. Gerard will retire in Reno, Nevada, where he intends to continue in public service as a volunteer with the Red Cross or another non-profit organization. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop at 5:30 p.m. tomorrow, December 2. Dave Ashton, who has ordered all the trees for many years, confirmed the Scouts were not able to buy as many Silvertips as they had hoped. Price hikes and limited availability of trees have been common everywhere on the West Coast. “The price increases [for customers] were modest in comparison to the cost increases [to the scouts]. We did not pass all the costs on, in hopes of providing the highest value trees available in the area,” said Ashton. The lot has plenty of Noble Firs, of all sizes, and still holds a decent supply of Douglas Firs too. Garlands, wreaths, and mistletoe are also available for purchase. To a person, the Scouts are overjoyed to be back selling trees in person, roaming the tree lot, and enjoying hot chocolate on the chilly nights. “I enjoy meeting the customers, and I would say I am a good salesman,” said Cub Scout Jackson Apodaca. “I like working with my friend Rob Ashton. Last year he got a badge for working 20 hours here, so he is just about the perfect Scout.” Apodaca added that his goal this year is to “work as many hours as I can without getting sleepy.” There will be no sales trailer this year to eliminate contact indoors between customers and the Scouts. Transactions are by debit or credit card only. Scouts and staff will wear masks when interacting with customers as a courtesy. articles.text: As the leaves begin to blow and the trails are carpeted in gold and red and brown, Camp Augusta is now settling down for a long winter’s nap. With acorns and pine needles scattered about the wood chips and a delicious feast shared by the staff who live on site, we were digesting our meal as well as our memories from this past summer. Though we were all grateful for a great many things, one shared theme was our gratitude for the reality of running summer camp for the hundreds of campers who played outside with us this, our 90th year! We all experienced a renewed sense of wish, wonder and surprise and many of our campers (and staff) were reminded of what it is to be a kid again. Hopefully the glow is still there. You know the one: when your camper returns from camp and they seem the same - yet different. A little bit dirtier, a little bit happier, a little bit more hmmm…. mature or centered within themselves? The golden glow starts to fade as the school year ensues and the fall arrives, but hopefully the embers are still there. Embers to rekindle the recent memories of a time not long ago when they were sleeping outside, running through the woods and basking in the glory of childhood. We truly have so much gratitude for the sounds of play returning to Augusta for our 90th year after such a quiet 2020. The laughter, the songs, the campfire, the hello hugs and the goodbye tears. The warm glow of the fire reflecting on young faces eager for the next adventure. Gratitude for you all, a community who recognizes the importance of the work Augusta does and your support through the last two years. And, to our anonymous donor who recently contributed $30,000 to kick start our end-of-year annual fundraising campaign. With gratitude and love being buzzwords this time of year, especially after the last two years of well, you know….Camp Augusta is thinking of all of you – grateful for your trust and confidence. For entrusting your children to our care to learn of a greater sense of self, without them really even realizing they are doing it, while here with us in the woods of Augusta. Thank you to our community – the old, the new, and to those we haven’t even met yet. Campingly yours, Randy Grayson Director, Camp Augusta p.s. articles.text: Shani Boyd, the Children’s Librarian at Piedmont Avenue Library, has many challenges to deal with in her new job and lots of energy to face them. She chose to specialize in children’s librarianship largely because she got so much satisfaction from reading fantasy when she was growing up. As early as middle school in Marin County she was serving as part of a teen advisory group for the local library. Still living in Marin, she drives to Oakland every day to develop programs for children, order materials, and support students in the community. It is a challenge during COVID to provide activities for kids while keeping them safe. Part of the job includes wiping down toys for check-out after they are used and before they go back out. She figures out how to do Storytime with proper distancing – not the kind of problems that usually come to mind when you think of a librarian’s job. But since August, Shani has been in the library every day, doing all that and taking her turn at staffing the circulation desk, too. Shani came to the Piedmont Avenue Branch library immediately after receiving a Master’s in Library Science degree from San Jose State, preceded by an undergraduate degree from University of the Pacific. She is still getting acquainted with the job and with her work team and the community. She has many ideas, much enthusiasm and she is eager to help keep Piedmont Avenue Library the community resource it has always been. When you are there, say hello and welcome Shani Boyd. Ruby Long is a neighbor whose work has appeared in local and national publications.

The Piedmont Recreation Department is offering a new after-school program called Shake, Rattle and Roll for elementary school-aged children, which offers opportunities for creative movement, music, and rhythmic exploration. Sign-ups are available for classes in January 2022, with three sessions throughout the school year. The program will be taught by Piedmont Adaptive P.E Specialist Raul Jorcino, and Nancy Henderson, a retired Albany Adaptive P.E Specialist. Jorcino and Henderson have more than 70 years of combined experience in adaptive physical education. “Both Nancy and Raul are truly amazing individuals, and we’ve formed this dream team. Nancy and I were able to create an inclusive program in the summer and school year [in Albany]. She and I have been working on what these programs will look like [in Piedmont],” Phalen said. The program is suited for children with neurodiverse needs in grades K-5. Henderson will teach the first two sessions, and Jorcino will teach session three. The program will be from 3:30 p.m. to 5 p.m. at Beach School. Session 1: Thursdays, January 13 - February 17 Session 2: Thursdays, March 3 - April 4 Session 3: Thursdays, April 21 - May 26. Classes will be limited to 10 children. Interested parents may call the Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 to enroll. Teen Sidekicks Teenaged “sidekicks” will be paired with campers in adaptive programing to help build relationships and strengthen children’s recreational skills. The Recreation Department is currently seeking volunteers ages 14 or older to commit to an entire session, Thursday afternoons for six weeks. Community service hours are available upon request, and volunteers may receive a letter of recommendation. Students interested in becoming a sidekick should contact Eva Phalen at ephalen@piedmont. ca.gov for an application

pages.text: Wednesday, December 1, 2021 7 Realtors extol Piedmont schools As the holidays approach, we’re often bombarded with requests for donations - all of them no less important than another, and many of them truly critical and worthy of our support. However, when it comes to the Piedmont community, the Piedmont Educational Foundation is unique in terms of what it provides locally, which works to make sure that our children have the benefit of music, art, science, theater, cultural enrichment programs, and so many other extras that make Piedmont schools the envy of the Bay Area. As Realtors who do a great deal of work inside the boundaries of Piedmont, we’re blessed to meet so many young families beginning their educational journeys, and we can attest to the fact that the number one reason these parents migrate to Piedmont is for the schools. Yes, the architecture is beautiful, the sense of community is unmatched, the social services are great, and the safe, treelined streets are all lovely draws, but it’s the schools that most drive their decision, and why the ongoing health of our public schools should be important to every homeowner in Piedmont, whether or not one still has school-aged children in attendance. In fact, the desirability of the public schools is directly tied into the property values of Piedmont’s homes; therefore, the need to continue to privately fund benefits everyone in town from an economic standpoint. From a personal vantage point, having navigated our kids through Piedmont schools and then on to college and then into the workforce thereafter, Sarah and I know that their formative years provided them with a solid educational base, a quest for knowledge, and life-long friendships that they’ll return to again and again. Which is why when Sarah and John Abel were asked to host the “Empty-Nester” party at their home, they willingly agreed, and why they hope you’ll consider making a donation to the Piedmont Educational Foundation as part of your annual giving practice. Your contribution is a gift to your children, everyone’s children, and those that follow. Happy holidays. Julie Gardner & Sarah Abel Compass Real Estate A cornucopia of thanks! Gratitude a’plenty from the Woods of Augusta As the leaves begin to blow and the trails are carpeted in gold and red and brown, Camp Augusta is now settling down for a long winter’s nap. With acorns and pine needles scattered about the wood chips and a delicious feast shared by the staff who live on site, we were digesting our meal as well as our memories from this past summer. Though we were all grateful for a great many things, one shared theme was our gratitude for the reality of running summer camp for the hundreds of campers who played outside with us this, our 90th year! We all experienced a renewed sense of wish, wonder and surprise and many of our campers (and staff) were reminded of what it is to be a kid again. Hopefully the glow is still there. You know the one: when your camper returns from camp and they seem the same - yet different. A little bit dirtier, a little bit happier, a little bit more hmmm…. mature or centered within themselves? The golden glow starts to fade as the school year ensues and the fall arrives, but hopefully the embers are still there. Embers to rekindle the recent memories of a time not long ago when they were sleeping outside, running through the woods and basking in the glory of childhood. We truly have so much gratitude for the sounds of play returning to Augusta for our 90th year after such a quiet 2020. The laughter, the songs, the campfire, the hello hugs and the goodbye tears. The warm glow of the fire reflecting on young faces eager for the next adventure. Gratitude for you all, a community who recognizes the importance of the work Augusta does and your support through the last two years. And, to our anonymous donor who recently contributed $30,000 to kick start our end-of-year annual fundraising campaign. With gratitude and love being buzzwords this time of year, especially after the last two years of well, you know….Camp Augusta is thinking of all of you – grateful for your trust and confidence. For entrusting your children to our care to learn of a greater sense of self, without them really even realizing they are doing it, while here with us in the woods of Augusta. Thank you to our community – the old, the new, and to those we haven’t even met yet. Campingly yours, Randy Grayson Director, Camp Augusta p.s. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Piedmont Avenue Library News Piedmont Avenue Branch Library update By Ruby Long Shani Boyd, the Children’s Librarian at Piedmont Avenue Library, has many challenges to deal with in her new job and lots of energy to face them. She chose to specialize in children’s librarianship largely because she got so much satisfaction from reading fantasy when she was growing up. As early as middle school in Marin County she was serving as part of a teen advisory group for the local library. Still living in Marin, she drives to Oakland every day to develop programs for children, order materials, and support students in the community. It is a challenge during COVID to provide activities for kids while keeping them safe. Part of the job includes wiping down toys for check-out after they are used and before they go back out. She figures out how to do Storytime with proper distancing – not the kind of problems that usually come to mind when you think of a librarian’s job. But since August, Shani has been in the library every day, doing all that and taking her turn at staffing the circulation desk, too. Shani came to the Piedmont Avenue Branch library immediately after receiving a Master’s in Library Science degree from San Jose State, preceded by an undergraduate degree from University of the Pacific. She is still getting acquainted with the job and with her work team and the community. She has many ideas, much enthusiasm and she is eager to help keep Piedmont Avenue Library the community resource it has always been. When you are there, say hello and welcome Shani Boyd. Ruby Long is a neighbor whose work has appeared in local and national publications.

Yasaman Ford, a PHS graduate in 2016, will be co-teaching the Reel Stories Women’s Filmmaking Weekend December 3-5 at the Ciel Creative Space in Berkeley. The popular and original program enables adult women to experience film production in an accelerated two and a half day event. Ford attended her first Camp Reel Stories program before her sophomore year at Piedmont High School and returned to its summer program for the next three years. It was at Reel Stories where her passion for film and feminism ignited. While attending UCLA’s School for Film and Television during the year, Ford would come home every summer to share her growing knowledge and experience of film with students through Reel Stories and Piedmont’s Summer Enrichment Program. Ford joined the Reel Stories Team as a Program Coordinator and Lead Media Instructor in March 2020. Founded in 2013 by Executive Director Esther Pearl, Reel Stories is the only female owned and operated non-profit film program for women in the country led by professionals. In addition to teaching filmmaking, Ford also creates and collaborates on film and digital media projects. Ford’s own work as a filmmaker ranges from narrative production design to directing documentaries, freelance motion graphics and editing. She aims to educate others, from toddlers to teenagers, on the importance of representation in the media. This year the program will be back in-person at the Ciel Creative Space in Berkeley, the only female-owned production studio. Signups for the December 3-5 weekend program are available online at: bit.ly/RSWoWe. articles.text: Over the last two years many of us have reflected on what it means to be a more inclusive society. As much as this heavy work starts within, it also begins with our little ones. Starting with our children, even the youngest, is a great way to change the narrative on what it means to see the world in a more inclusive way. There are many holidays celebrated this time of year, and I am reminded of how Christmas can define the “season.” However, this is an excellent opportunity to expose children to different cultures, practices and traditions. Many holiday celebrations incorporate storytelling, or histories, to pass on traditions. Exploring celebrations different from our own offer children the opportunity to not only experience different traditions but to also see common values - family, love, respect and honor. This exploration allows children to develop an understanding of the world around them and that is more inclusive of others. Here are a few tips to help families of young children have a deeper exploration of “holiday seasons:” • Learn about the holidays. Do some research on different holidays and discover their origin and why they are celebrated. • Explore different cultures year-round. Cultural traditions are all year long. • PBS.org (https://www.pbs. org/parents/search/ages-all/ topics-all/shows-all/types-all/ keyword-cultural+diversity) has great suggestions for that exploration. Read children’s books about different holidays and traditions. Oakland Public Library (https://oaklandlibrary.bibliocommons. com/v2/search?query=cultural%20holidays&search Type=smart&ga=2.144097783. 33607171.1638227251-4022453 • • • 18.1638227251) has a fantastic collection of books for all ages. Consider attending a local holiday festival. While you’re there, look for things that are similar to your holiday traditions. 510 Families (https:// www.510families.com/calendar/) is a great resource for local events. Visit cultural centers or museums. Explore different holiday celebrations. Visit with people that celebrate different holidays. At Children’s Fairyland we include many holiday traditions into our Fairy Winterland (https:// childrensfairyland.brushfire.com/ fairyland/518645) celebration and will continue to do so as we endeavor to learn and change. I hope for you, and Fairyland, that exploring these activities helps build a collective push toward a more inclusive world and create a community that shares deeper joys, together. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling. I learned the terms to be able to talk about statistics well enough, and familiarized myself with some equations and how to use the calculator. Although scared and prepared to apologize my way out the door halfway through the session, I was able to help, and I learned a valuable thing about education. Many struggling students just can’t get started and quickly get stumped and quit. For these students, having a tutor sit with them for an hour to work may be all they need. My statistics student turned a D into a B- and was able to graduate. We were able to get to the crux of the material and figure out where the limits of his knowledge were and learn what questions to ask. Many people can play the role of a tutor in cases like this, although parents often have a conflict of interest in taking on the role. Some parents lament that they themselves use Algebra or Geometry in their careers daily and consider themselves adept but can’t help. Students may feel that school is the only place where their parents are not the boss. A younger sibling may be able to help a student who works better in groups or learns through speaking and listening. One key in math is to say out loud the names of the concepts and terms that are being used. For example, in Algebra, a set of more than one equation is called a “System of Equations.” Just saying that out loud can help with a discussion about it. Talking it out can result in a student realizing a mistake mid-sentence, as the words get stuck on their lips. I recommend creating a list of each type of question and concept and a list of terms with examples and descriptions. Turning numbers into letters can be tough, but well worth it.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. Piedmont’s basketball team fell 76-62 to St. Ignatius in San Francisco for its season-opener on Saturday, November 27. The Wildcats compete in the Central Coast Section. “We just didn’t come ready to play, we got outworked on both ends of the floor,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “We had 2-3 bad minutes in the second quarter and that was the ball game. We’re preaching defense and will go back to the drawing board.” A.J. Harris led the way with 28 points, while JoJo Murphy had a difficult game with 18 points after returning from an ankle injury. “A.J. had a great night; he was 11 of 16 from the floor. JoJo hadn’t practiced in around two weeks and had a tough night shooting. He was short on many shots that he typically makes, so perhaps his ankle wasn’t all the way there,” said Spencer. St. Ignatius did well to move the ball around to find open shooters, and their tall center managed to block three shots and force Piedmont into difficult shots around the basket. “They were really well coaches and very disciplined. They have 12 seniors and they were able to maintain composure and work really well together,” said Spencer. Piedmont trailed 14-11 at the end of the first quarter, but St. Ignatius blew the game open with a 41-27 lead by halftime. The Wildcats held a 58-46 lead to start the fourth, and closed out the victory at 76-62. “They are in a tough league with some big schools and are a great team to play. articles.text: Bryan Gardere, a PHS alum, began coaching Piedmont’s girls basketball team prior to the 2002- 2003 season. He arrived with a fire in his eye and mission to create a respected basketball program in the East Bay. His team won the first State Championship in school history, then added a second title one year later. In his 19 hears at the helm, his teams have also won four North Coast Section championships and four league titles. His current team includes at least three players drawing college interest. When asked for his comments upon entering his 19th season, he laughed and replied, “That’s crazy, man. I haven’t even talked about it. I remember starting just like it was yesterday. Those were some really good times. It feels like it hasn’t been that long, but when you think about it, we’ve had maybe 12 athletic directors, 4-5 principals, hundreds of kids. The kids on this year’s team weren’t even born! “I didn’t know what high school basketball was about when I came here, I walked into a very solid team. To start something Bryan Gardere has helped send a long list of student-athletes to college. and still be is strange to think about. I can’t complain for one second,” he said. It all started in 2002 when the Paris twins, Courtney and Ashley Paris and their family moved to Piedmont from Modesto. Piedmont had never won any championships, but it changed quickly. The Paris sisters helped catapult Piedmont into the limelight and led the Highlanders to consecutive State titles in 2004 and 2005. During that time Piedmont won the North Coast Section in four consecutive years, from 2003 through 2006. At different times, Piedmont was the No. 1 team in the country in 2004 and 2005. Those years included three more Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame members: Logan Rawlings went onto the University of Virginia in 2004, while Annie Crangle joined the University of Wisconsin and Chazny Morris signed with University of Kansas City in 2006. “We had five or six Division 1 athletes on the team. We were ranked No. 1 in the country; we had 50-60 college coaches in the gym at one time because the Paris twins were so in-demand, So many people got involved in the community. For our first home game we had a line leading out of the gym, up the stairs and around the theater to get in. Everyone in the town tried to fit in. The JV game played in front of a sold-out gym; it was pretty amazing,” Gardere recalled. Gardere recalled having ice cream sandwiches at the home of Bebe Rawlings, founder of Otis Spunkmeyer cookies and the father of Logan. “It was Mr. Otis Spunkmeyer himself. We would have some of the best cookie ice-cream sandwich parties at his house. We would go to his house. He’d bake fresh cookies and put scoops of Bryan Gardere has among the most wins for active coaches in the state. Bryan Gardere oversees another session of his popular Piedmont Basketball Academy. Bryan Gardere in 2018 with former players Kristen Seyranian (left) and Jasmyne Huggins. Staff Photos Bryan Gardere is entering his 19th year as head coach of Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team, building a winning culture at Binks Rawlings Gym. He took over as head coach ahead of the 2002-2003 season. ice cream in between. It was special,” Gardere reminisced. Gardere spent his high school days in the halls of PHS and in the gym as a member of the PHS varsity. After graduating in 1994 he pursued a professional basketball career. He accepted the job to coach the girls’ basketball team after playing in Ecuador’s top basketball league, and playing on teams in Germany and France. Former Cal men’s coach Dick Kuchen knew how remarkable the Paris twins were, and offered to help coach the team, functioning as a mentor to Gardere. He stayed on for five years. “It was awesome as a first-year coach to have his knowledge to help me navigate through being a head coach,” said Gardere. “He was my assistant, respectfully, because he didn’t want the [head coaching] job and just wanted to stay involved in the game.” “He was invaluable in helping a young me. I got a crash-course on how to be a high-level coach, and it was a blessing. There wasn’t a situation he hadn’t been in. He helped me become a better coach in such a fast amount of time. People have to wait years for the knowledge he was giving me, and it was my first year,” he added. Comparing himself as a coach when he arrived in 2003 to now, Gardere believes the 2004 and 2005 teams could have won a National Title. It’s funny to think about because all my alumni say I’m super soft now. I think with time and experience, you learn a lot and recognize game situations more quickly and try more savvy things. It just takes time,” said Gardere with a chuckle. Gardere has helped send a considerable number of players to play in college. In addition to players already mentioned, the full list includes: Casey Morris, Texas Tech in 2008; Dominique Hamilton, San Jose State in 2008; Pepper Kuo, Queens College in 2009; Sarah Tamulski, Temple in 2009; Clara Tate, Mount Holyoke College in 2009; Andrea Chenier, New Mexico State/Sac State in 2010; Saidah Allen, Fresno State/ UTEP in 2011; Jamie Wallace, Colby College in 2011; Lauren Seyranian, UC Davis in 2014; Photo courtesy of SF Gate Bryan Gardere with his mentor Dick Kuchen (left) in 2005. Kuchen was a head coach at Cal, Notre Dame, and Yale. JoNae Gonzales, Sonoma State in 2014; Ameela Li, University of the Pacific in 2015; Kelea Pickeral-Dennis, University of Kansas/San Francisco State in 2015; Ny’Dajah Jackson, Providence College/Youngstown State in 2016; Jasmyne Huggins, Menlo College in 2019; Ashley Gao, University of Chicago in 2019; Maddy Meadows, Biola University in 2020; Naimah Thompson, Laney College in 2020; and Kai Johnson, Weber State in 2021. “That’s a long list, right? Casey Morris just wrote a children’s book and got her Doctorate. Chaz went on to be the alltime leading scorer at U of KC; Andrea Chenier is now a Stanford conditioning trainer; Ashley Gao is doing great at Chicago, Jasmyne just scored 20 [points and had 12 rebounds for Menlo. It is so awesome to be a small part of their journey,” said Gardere. Now moving into the 2021- 2022 season, Gardere brings back a lineup with NCAA-caliber talent in juniors Trinity Zamora and Maddy Mills, and sophomore Natalia Martinez. “Some people think Trinity is the best player in Northern California, and she’s on our team. Maddy is playing outstanding as well,” he said. Gardere’s team begins its season this week at the Bryan Ayer Classic in Lompoc in Central California from December 2-4. PHS will open competition against Santa Barbara tomorrow at 4:30 p.m.

articles.text: Musicians Steve Oda, Michael Lewis and Pushpa Oda will perform a selection of North Indian classical music on Saturday, December 11 at Piedmont Center for the Arts beginning 7 p.m. The music will be followed by a dance performance by Kali Futnani, a senior teacher at Bharata Kalanjali in Berkeley. Futnani began her dance training at Kalanjali in Berkeley, which was founded by K.P and Katherine Kunhiraman. She has a BFA from Kalakshetra College of Fine Arts in Chennai, India. Kali continued her training under K.P. Yesodha in Chennai for six years, performing with the company throughout India before returning to the Bay Area. Bharatanatyam is a South Indian classical dance style that was performed in the temples of Tamil Nadu for thousands of years before coming to the stage. Bharatanatyam has both rhythmic and dramatic aspects. The theory of rasa, the nature of the aesthetics as transcendental and emotional experience, is central to all Indian arts. Through movement set to rhythmic patterns and storytelling through hand gestures and Kali Futnani expression, the audience and the performer have a shared experience through art. Tickets are $20 at the door, and $10 for students with high school or college identification. All events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require proof of vaccination and proper masking while indoors.

California Revels dives into the Age of Sail, blending 19th Century London with folklore and traditions from the Caribbean and Gullah Islands in an odyssey across the Atlantic. From sea chanties, mermaids, and Christmas carols to Jonkonnu and Papa Bois, the performances will celebrate the Winter Solstice. Audiences of all ages will appreciate the glories of traditional music, dance, ritual and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance,” all with top Bay Area musicians, actors, and performers. La Sirène is directed by Amy Marie Haven and written by Jeff Raz. California Revels is led by Artistic Director Rene Collins and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Christopher Bryden is Children’s Music Director. Choreographed by Jeri Reed. Tickets are $15-$75. Futnani began her dance training at Kalanjali in Berkeley, which was founded by K.P and Katherine Kunhiraman. She has a BFA from Kalakshetra College of Fine Arts in Chennai, India. Bharatanatyam is a South Indian classical dance style that was performed in the temples of Tamil Nadu for thousands of years before coming to the stage. articles.text: Art review by Jaime Robles The Art of Banksy, a collection of iconic prints and art by the anonymous UK street artist, opened at San Francisco’s Palace of Fine Arts this month and its stay has been extended through Sunday, February 27, due to popular demand. The exhibition includes many of Banksy’s most famous works. The little girl watching a heartshaped balloon float away, a chimpanzee coiffed and bejewelled like Queen Elizabeth, the street protestor throwing a bouquet of flowers. There are helicopters adorned with huge pink bows, squads of military wearing “happy face” masks, and rats. Lots of rats doing all kinds of ratty things. “If you feel dirty, insignificant or unloved, then rats are a good role model. They exist without permission, they have no respect for the hierarchy of society, and they have sex 50 times a day.” So reads one of the many Banksy-attributed quotes stenciled on the black walls of the winding corridors that run through the exhibition space. Photos by Jaime Robles “Laugh Now” screen print from The Art of Banksy. This piece shows the characteristic soft edge of the spray can paint and stencil technique used by Banksy in his street art. Banksy is a wonderful artist. His work was one of the earliest and most representative of street art that used stenciled rather than freehand spray can drawing. He has stated that he used stencils so that he could more quickly produce his art and escape the police patrolling the streets that make up his canvases. Stencils gave his work a distinctive and recognizable style. Banksy also has a sharp satiric mind and passionate beliefs about poverty and the cruelty it endures under the uncaring machinations of a capitalist State. Part of his genius is his ability to convey those beliefs in simple and succinct black-and-white images. His art is both impressionistic and precise at the same time, giving it an immediate and arresting quality. The Art of Banksy is a kind of catalog of the guerrilla exhibitions that Banksy organized or was part of during his early days as a street artist. And it adds to the history of street art as a movement within the UK, a collective in-your-face protest of politics and the politics of art. The effort and the imagination are impressive not only for this singular artDorothy undergoes a basket check. ist but for the contributing young street artists themselves, whose work and passion are surely underrated by the slick purveyors of taste and high art within the UK – and the US. A video interview with Banksy’s early days screen printer, Ben Eine, is projected on several screens throughout the show. Eine explains the history and process of the prints while showing his own impressive display of tattoo art on his forearms and neck. The artwork has been gathered from collectors reportedly from around the globe, but the exhibition is unauthorized. On his personal website page called Product Recall, Banksy lists the exhibition along with others shown worldwide from Budapest to Tel Aviv to Las Vegas. The anonymous Banksy. The dollar cost of the entrance fee to each exhibition is listed and an opening paragraph reads enigmatically: “Members of the public should be aware there has been a recent spate of Banksy exhibitions none of which are consensual. They‘ve been organised entirely without the artist’s knowledge or involvement. Please treat them accordingly.” While it’s true the exhibition entrance fee comes in at a hefty $39.99, complete with a capitalist classic, the penny discount, and you have to exit through a gift shop of Banksy cups, T-shirts and food concessions, the exhibition itself is a lot of fun. Full of wry truth-telling and humor that is both desperate and loving. There has always been poignancy to street art. And great generosity. All of these are in full display at in Banksy’s art. For a cheaper ride and a smallscreen experience, you can also try visiting Banksy’s website. It’s well worth it. In compliance with the City of San Francisco’s vaccine mandate, visitors of The Art of Banksy will be required to present proof of full vaccination with valid ID in order to attend the exhibit. Masks are mandatory for all attendees. Please consult the website for additional information on COVID- 19 protocols.

articles.text: A concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts last week was of such magnitude that for the first time in my life, I find myself literally speechless. The concert on Saturday afternoon, November 20, was sponsored by the Kodaly Foundation for Music Education. A young pianist from Indonesia, Jessica Suandrianna, was the featured soloist. This is a name and a musician you will want to remember. Only 28 years old, she proved herself to be masterful in every way. She has all the technique a pianist could ever hope for. That she puts it to the service of the highest levels of artistry is extraordinary. Everything about her playing is artistic and profound. This is an extraordinary combination and rather unknown to musicians of her generation. Jessica walks onto the stage with a simplicity and a dignity that is disarming. There is an economy of movement which produces the greatest results. The rarely heard piano Sonata by Edvard Grieg was notable for elegant voicing, absolute independence of the hands, and a resonant tone that sounded orchestral. After the Grieg sonata came four piano pieces by Brahms which transported to us into a German dream land. Once again, the piano became an orchestra. There was will-of-the-wisp lightness and then, quick as a cat, came the thunder and the lightning – and all the pastel colors in between. Pathos and romanticism were brought to the fore in two nocturnes by Frederick Chopin, and then another change of pace with Debussy’s L’ile joyeuse. Then once again came a change of mood and color with a new composition by the Indonesian composer Ananda Sukarlan. This extraordinary program was brought to a conclusion by another new composition entitled Tryptich of an Encounter, written for piano four hands by the Belgian pianist- teacher Gilbert de Greeve who was in the Center to join Ms. Suandrianna. He was a teacher of hers and remains her mentor. Quite frankly, their performance was the finest example of four hand piano playing I have ever heard. They played as one. The interplay between the two was as beautiful to watch as it was to listen to. Mentor Gilbert de Greeve (left) joined his brilliant student Jessica Suandrianna for some 4-hands piano works at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, November 20.
articles.title: Masterful pianist visits Piedmont

articles.text: Opening reception on Saturday, Dec. 4 at 5 p.m. Four East Bay artists will present an exhibition entitled A Boundless Moment at Piedmont Center for the Arts this weekend, Saturday and Sunday, December 4-5, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. The exhibit will be open to the public again the following weekend, December 11-12. The exhibit will showcase the works of Carl Heyward, Akiko Suzuki, Usha Shukla, and Colleen Gianatiempo. Heyward is the recipient of a National Endowment for the Arts grant and a former Masters of Fine Arts instructor at the San Francisco Academy of Art University. His work has been featured at various art galleries in the Bay Area and internationally. Suzuki is a textile and mixed media artist based in San Francisco. Since 2014, she has particArtist. Colleen Giantiempo Artist Carl Heyward ipated in Global Art Project with partner Heyward. “My work expresses the invisible nature of thought, of skin sensation, the poetry of Love and Eros or the presentiments that occur prior to thought. Intuitive works are born from everyday life as are novels,” Suzuki said. “The words borne out of the flood of my imagery become poetry and are visualized in works as abstractions through paint, collage, sewing and fiber works.” Shukla was raised in New Delhi, India, where the vibrant colors of the Indian countryside greatly influenced her artwork. She completed a graduate program at the Academy of Art University in San Francisco, with a focus on painting. She paints primarily large abstracts in vivid colors and has a unique process of “mark-making.” Gianatiempo is a mixed media artist, educator, and designer living in the East Bay. “My journey as an artist began when I was 3 years old. I remember cutting up family photos and drawing on walls with lipstick. I learned early on that it’s possible to express the world around me in different ways, and this is where my passion began,” Gianatiempo said. “Nature is my main influence as I always marvel about the design and beauty it beholds,” she said. “I work in many mediums and thrive most when I can experiment and discover new techniques. I have been told that I am the Mary Poppins of art supplies.” An opening reception will be held this Saturday, December 4, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. Gallery hours will be open to the public, with no reservation required, on Sunday, December 5 from noon to 3 p.m., and again on December 11 and 12 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required at all Piedmont Center for the Arts events.

articles.text: Olivia Wilde and Oscar Isaac in Life Itself. Life Itself, written and directed by Dan Fogelman, is framed by the trope known as the unreliable narrator, meaning a narrator whose credibility is brought into question. It is a familiar plot device used in literature and film and is oft repeated like a mantra in Fogelman’s story. The film opens with Will Dempsey (Oscar Isaac) standing at the counter of a small coffee shop. Taking his cup of coffee, he adds tabs of Xanax, sips, and then begins to sing and talk loudly as the owner and a barista push him toward the door. It’s immediately established that he is not only the protagonist of the story, but strangely quirky and untethered from his surroundings. The essential question posed in this brief setup is, why? What has brought him to this point in his life? The next scene takes place in the office of Will’s therapist (Annette Bening). She is questioning him about his recent mental health; his answers in previous sessions have always been oblique and evasive. But today he grudgingly begins to talk about his courtship and then marriage to Abbey (Olivia Wilde), which is revealed in a long flashback. She was a university student and he a writer. At a house party they sit on the front porch steps and she asks him why he has never asked her out. Will tells her that if he crossed that threshold there would be no turning back regarding his devotion to her. As is revealed, their relationship is heartbreakingly intimate, joyful, and Will is shown telling Abbey that he will dedicate his life to making her life more than wonderful. And it is Abbey, holding her senior thesis, who introduces the idea that becomes the film’s mantra: it isn’t just the literary narrator who is unreliable but it is life itself. Meanwhile, the therapist presses Will to confront his recent events and their unexpected and tragic outcome, one that involves a truth that is more than he can bear. His affect is evasive, shrouded with emotional revetments, and a head-shaking resistance against a traumatic memory that he distorts in order to cope. In the many flashbacks, the lengthy vignettes, and the dramatic pauses, each is filtered through Will’s prism thus making it impossible for the audience to rely on what he has shared as being either truthful or remotely normative. It’s at this point that the story shifts to Will’s 21-year-old daughter, Dylan (Olivia Cooke), who is living with her grandfather (Mandy Patinkin). For reasons that are self-evident she is overwhelmed by a sense of angst, her default response to her life one of anger and resistance. This brief chapter ends with her sitting on a bus stop bench in the middle of the night and slowly drifting off into a soft, barely conscious sleep. Now, abruptly, Life Itself makes a complete change of location (Spain), language (Spanish with subtitles), and characters. The setting is a bucolic olive plantation owned by Senior Saccione (Antonio Banderas), a wealthy single man. We are introduced to Javier Gonzalez (Sergio Peris-Mencheta) and Isabel (Laia Costa). Javier works on the plantation and Isabel is his new wife. They live in a casita near the main house. This narrative is straightforward, though subtle hints convey that possible heartbreak is just within reach. Fogelman is a master of the lachrymose. The audience can intuit that regardless of all appearances, life is not linear; rather, it’s a gestalt of various directions, making the point that Abbey is an unreliable narrator. One last point: Recall that the script for Life Itself was written by Fogelman, who created the theme of the unreliable narrator. And it is Fogelman who inserts unexpected tragedies before abruptly flipping the narrative to one that at least promises some clarity. It’s as if Fogelman wanted to create a film that is more like a novel in structure and exposition. He crafts a kind of tale that allows him to examine certain themes that thread their way through our lives, always different in texture though also universal in experience. I give Fogelman kudos for this film, for risking all to examine life in all its vagaries. For those who love film as a way to tell stories and mirror life’s experiences, I say, go see this film. Then ponder and wrestle with its strengths and its weaknesses. Life Itself. Directed by Dan Fogelman. Starring Oscar Isaac, Olivia Wilde, Antonio Banderas. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. articles.text: First things first: Win Win is not a sports film, though the title and ad posters seem to promise a plot that revolves around a team and its coaches. It’s much more. While it does focus on high school wrestling, the film is never formulaic. It is not about winning on the mats, or about a weak team transformed into a group of wunderkins; rather, it is about flawed yet decent people who out of kindness fashion an improbable family. Begin with Paul Giamatti. If you’ve not seen him in “Sideways,” then make a point of renting this film. It was his breakthrough movie, launching his career as more than a minor character actor. Giamatti would be the first to acknowledge that he is not your typical leading man: sad-eyed, overweight, and balding. Yet he is so good – brilliant, really – at portraying certain characters that it’s always a delight to watch someone so talented work. Giamatti relishes the role of Mike Flaherty: a struggling lawyer with few clients, a volunteer high school wrestling coach, married to Jackie, nicely portrayed by Amy Ryan, father to two girls, and living in a modest home. While the movie has been billed as a comedy, it is much more. Win Win is essentially about good people and situations in which they do the best they can while realizing even their best may not be enough. Until it is. Unexpectedly, into the Flaherty home comes a teenage kid, Kyle, played by Alex Shaffer. As Mike soon discovers, he is a gifted wrestler who is also troubled – his mother is in rehab and his grandfather is living in a nursing home. He has run away from home, hoping to move in with his grandfather no matter that he is a stranger to him. Mike convinces Jackie that they should take in the boy until his mother can be found. She believes they now have Eminem living in their basement, a delinquent rapper who is beyond help. Writer/director Tom McCarthy does not portray Kyle stereotypically, which makes the movie far richer and more engaging. The film soon evolves into a soft, subtle, very human tale, serious and comedic. The ensemble of actors is superb, to include Kyle’s mom, Cindy, nicely rendered by Melanie Lynskey, as well as the veteran actor Burt Young, who plays the aging grandfather suffering from early dementia. Win Win is proof that small movies are still being made that exemplify excellent storytelling, deeply human, filled with delightful, well-intentioned, imperfect people. Win Win. Directed by Tom McCarthy. Starring Paul Giamatti, Amy Ryan, Bobby Cannvavale, Jeffrey Tambor, Melanie Lynskey and Burt Young. 2 hrs., 27 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Shelby, the star pooch in A Dog’s Way Home, was discovered in a dog shelter after she was saved from a Tennessee garbage dump. As far as the kids are concerned, A Dog’s Way Home finds the PG sweet spot and stays there. They’ll take to it like, well, ducks to water. But then it’s a story about a nifty dog named Bella and her owner, Lucas (Jonah Hauer King), a med student living with his mom, Teri (Ashley Judd). Lucas and his fellow med student, Olivia (Alexandra Shipp), find Bella as a pup, living with cats and kittens under an abandoned wreck of a house, and it’s Lucas who takes the wiggly, excitable, playful pooch home. She is literally a rescue dog; the house is about to be bulldozed. A year goes by, Bella grows up, and is spotted by a villainous animal control guy, Chuck (John Cassini), who makes it his mission to catch her on the street, unleashed. He claims she’s a pit bull. Worried that Bella could be impounded and even put down, Teri and Lucas send her to stay briefly with relatives in Farmington, New Mexico, while they search for a place to live outside of the city limits and out of Chuck’s jurisdiction. Bella is, of course, homesick, misses Lucas and Terri, and at the first opportunity makes a break for it, not realizing that she is 400 miles away from home. And so begins Bella’s twoyear adventure. It proves to be a mildly harrowing journey that involves humans, a pack of stalking wolves, two men who want to adopt her, an orphaned mountain lion cub that tags along, an avalanche, and learning to survive on leftovers in garbage bins. But Bella determinedly makes her way toward home and Lucas. Kids will love all of it. Plus, the filmmakers, having adapted A Dog’s Way Home from the bestselling novel by Bruce Cameron, decide to give the film a Bella voice over (by Bryce Dallas Howard) allowing her to share her impressions of all that she encounters. No worries regarding animals talking. Kids are totally on board with anthropomorphizing animals. Remember a Disneyesque small wooden boy and an iconic mouse. Plus. humans talk to dogs all the time and swear they get an answer topped off with a wagging tail. This is a family friendly film with a great story. Bella meets lots of kind people along the way. A Dog’s Way Home. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG. Now streaming

articles.text: The live action feature The Kid Who Would Be King opens with a brief animated prologue of the Arthurian legend and then skips to present day England, the setting for this fresh, energetic tale. At its center are a 12-yearold boy, Alex (Louis Ashbourne Serkis), and his best bud Bedders (Dean Chaumoo). Their first year in secondary school has just begun. Two bullies, Kaye and Lance (Rhianna Dorris, Tom Taylor) have singled out Alex and Bedders to torment. When one of their confrontations is broken up by a school administrator the four are given detention. In the late afternoon, Alex is on his way home when is chased by Kaye and Lance. He runs into an abandoned construction site to hide and it’s there that he discovers a sword sticking out of a block of concrete, and, grasping the hilt, he manages to pull the blade free. He later shows it to Bedders, and they conclude that it is the Excalibur, the sword of King Arthur. The next day, a mysterious kid comes to the school, and seeks out Alex and Bedders. He tells them that he is actually the wizard Merlin (Angus Imrie), who has the power to age backward. When Alex is skeptical, the strange boy transforms himself into the older Merlin (Patrick Stewart), and he tells the boys that Alex is a descendent of King Arthur. He has come to ask for help to defeat the newly awakened wicked sorceress, Morgana (Rebecca Ferguson), Arthur’s half-sister, who, with her army of demon knights, is about to leave her underworld during a solar eclipse and lay waste to the world. It’s also her mission the find and take possession of the Excalibur. Merlin explains that the only hope for England is Alex. With the Excalibur, he knights Bedders, and with optimism includes Kaye and Lance. The four, discussing the chivalric code, in all its guileless decency, form what will resemble the Arthurian round table. They pledge that they will defend the world from evil and are then trained by Merlin in swordsmanship. And thus begins what will be an epic, heroic adventure during which they confront Morgana and do battle with her demon knights. Unexpectedly the Excalibur is destroyed, but then restored. Alex also learns the history of his family, and his connection to Arthur/ The Kid Who Would Be King is an exciting and compelling saga with a rousing conclusion that ends with the entire student body at Alex’s school is knighted and joins in the battle against Morgana. Tweens and newbie teens will be captivated by the story, filled with action, but absent even a drop of blood. The Kid Who Would Be King. Directed by Joe Cornish. Starring Louis Ashbourne Serkis, Rhianna Dorris, Patrick Stewart, Tom Taylor. 2 hrs. Rated PG.

For the sake of everyone in your family, don’t avoid these “taboo” topics. You’ll need to be careful about approaching these subjects with your parents. Mention ahead of time that you’d like to talk to them about their future plans and reassure them that you want to understand their wishes, so their affairs will be taken care of as they would like. If your parents are agreeable, choose a location comfortable for them and ask whom they might like to invite (or not invite). Then, think about how to open the conversation, preferably not with what they want to do with their money – this could be interpreted as your seeking information about your inheritance or being skeptical about their financial decisions. Instead, build a broad-based discussion about their vision for their aging years. articles.text: Barbara Fox Roach passed away peacefully in her sleep in her beloved Piedmont home on Monday, November 8, 2021, after a courageous six-month battle with cancer. She lived a long, extraordinary life, capped by the celebration of her 90th birthday in June. Barbara was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on June 2, 1931, the youngest of seven siblings and the only daughter of John Raymond Fox and Elsie Warren Fox. Despite an age difference that spanned 21 years, she remained close to all of her brothers: Les, Joe, Art, Gil, Gene, and Jerry. Her childhood years were a challenge during the Depression, but growing up on a ranch helped shape Barbara into the ambitious, determined, and courageous young woman she became. At the age of thirteen, she moved in with another family, where she earned her room and board as a nanny and house cleaner until her graduation from Sheridan High School in 1949. Barbara attended Cottey College in Missouri, then transferred to the University of Wyoming, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in English in 1953 and was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. Barbara then moved west to San Francisco and became a stewardess for United Airlines. At a time when commercial flying was still in its nascency, she enjoyed long, friendly encounters with the likes of Walt Disney, Gregory Peck, and John Steinbeck. It was in San Francisco where she met the first love of her life, Justin M. Roach Jr., while Justin was attending Stanford Law School. They married in San Francisco in 1959 and then moved to Piedmont in 1960, where they raised their family and lived the rest of their lives. Justin began a long and distinguished legal career with the Oakland law firm that would eventually become Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. Barbara and Justin enjoyed a 28-year marriage until Justin’s death in 1987. In 2005, Barbara met the second love of her life, Arne Kalmar, also of Piedmont. The two enjoyed 10 wonderful years together, traveling the world, vacationing at their homes in Carmel and Palm Desert, and playing golf with friends at Claremont Country Club in Oakland and Monterey Peninsula Country Club in Pebble Beach, until Arne’s passing in 2016. A life-long Republican and philanthropist, Barbara contributed to numerous charitable, community, and political organizations, including the Cancer League, the Oakland Museum, the Russian National Orchestra, the San Francisco Opera, the Oakland Symphony, the Oakland Zoo, and the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West in Cody, Wyoming. As a member of the board of the Oakland Zoo, Barbara played an important role in the zoo’s fundraising efforts and its transformation into a world-class institution. Her passion for politics eventually led her to work on the re-election campaign of Pete Wilson to the U.S. Senate and to Barbara Roach, a resident of Piedmont for 60 years, died on November 8 at age 90. become a member of the Lincoln Club of Northern California and the Media Research Group. Barbara will be remembered for her lively wit, vivacity, and friendly nature. She was always an engaged listener who loved to share her observations through colorful vignettes of people and events. She also possessed a steady and insatiable curiosity in past and present issues – a trait cultivated by years of traveling the world with experts and loved ones. Not surprisingly, she had numerous interests and hobbies that ranged from orchid growing and needlepointing to playing tennis and golf. She remained an avid reader of fiction and nonfiction throughout her life and loved the opera as much as she loved a crisp, morning walk. Few could ever keep pace with her, even in her later years. Barbara was devoted to her four children – Justin Roach III (Dianne Peebles Roach), Kristin Roach Roeth (George), Steven Roach (Erica Heinsen) and David Roach (Christi Nielsen). “Barbar” loved and adored her eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren: Jessica Roach, Justin Roach IV, and James Roach; Justin Henry “Hank” Roeth (Haley), Megan Roeth, Jack Roeth and Everett Roeth; Emmett Roach and Renée Roach; Dillon Roach and Nathan Nielsen, and the newest additions to the family tree, Jeanette Roeth and Justin Henry Roeth II. Barbara was the matriarch of a large, loving family that will always remember her for her courage, fortitude, love, and grace. Barbara’s family is eternally grateful for the love and support of all of Barbara’s close friends who were by her side physically and spiritually these last several months. In particular, the family would like to extend its profound thanks and deep appreciation to Amy McClaskey and Elizabeth Vigo, who were her companions and caregivers until the very end. A private memorial service and celebration of life for family and friends is planned for January 8, 2022. Donations in Barbara’s memory may be made to the Oakland Zoo, the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West, or a charity of choice.

articles.text: Bill Blackwell died peacefully on Thanksgiving in the Piedmont home he shared with his wife, Marjorie for 41 years. Born William Dinsmore Blackwell in Indianapolis, Indiana on August 25, 1939, he was the son of Raymond Earl Blackwell and Dorothy Dinsmore Bloom. At age 5, his family moved to Louisville, Kentucky. An architect by profession, Bill had a diverse and successful career that included numerous design and planning projects in the U.S. and abroad, as well as other creative activities, over a span of 60 years. His work was his life. From a small public high school in Anchorage, Kentucky, he won an appointment to the U.S. Naval Academy in 1947. After completing 2½ years at the Academy, he transferred to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to pursue his dream of becoming an architect. He received a bachelor’s degree in architecture from MIT in 1953 and was immediately inducted into the Army. As a young sergeant in Korea, he was able to contribute to the design and relocation of Signal Corps facilities under wartime conditions. Following discharge, he returned to Louisville and worked for three years with a prominent architectural firm. His projects included a master plan for the University of Louisville, designs of a student union building and of a large Methodist church. In 1958, he moved to California and, under the GI Bill, earned a master’s degree in architecture from the University of California, Berkeley. In 1960, Bill joined the architectural firm of Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill in San Francisco. Over six years, his projects included design of the structural research laboratory at the UC Richmond Field Station, a complex radiochemistry laboratory at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, and a conceptual plan for the redevelopment of Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House to the Capitol in Washington, DC. In 1966, he joined the San Fra ncisco Redevelopment Agency to work on planning and design of the Western Addition Redevelopment Area. His efforts resulted in deleting widening of Turk Street and reducing parking requirements, making 17 blocks of housing economically feasible. Bill recognized early on the need for more housing in the City. In 1972, he wrote a growth scenario for San Francisco, based on a grid pattern, that would enable more people to live within walking distance of neighborhood shops, parks, transportation and other amenities. He also drafted a zoning ordinance, passed by the San Francisco Planning Commission, that allows higher densities through development of narrow-lot townhouses. Bill was a craftsman who designed and built his own furniture. He had a one-man show of his furniture designs as part of the Bay Area Art Explosion in 1967. Subsequently, he was Bill Blackwell at a recent 4th of July Parade in Piedmont. invited to join the Market Street Joint Venture Architects and was a lead designer in 1969 of the traffic signals and other items of Market Street’s outdoor furniture, some of it still in place. articles.text: James (“Jim”) Chapple Soper, a longtime resident of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully with his children by his side on November 15, 2021. He was 92. Born on January 15, 1929 in Billings, Montana, he was the son of Erastus Burrows Soper III and Dorothy Chapple Soper. Jim developed many lifelong friendships at Stanford and remained an active alum. While in his third year at Stanford University School of Law, Jim met the love of his life, Suzanne Simon. Following his service, Jim returned to live in Piedmont and began his career as an attorney in Oakland. Jim and Suzi raised their family on Oakmont Avenue, the street where Jim grew up and where his parents continued to live into their senior years. Jim and Suzi lived in two houses on Oakmont. When they outgrew one, they moved across the street. They dearly loved their Oakmont neighbors. Jim began his career at Fitzgerald Abbott & Beardsley (now Donahue Fitzgerald) in Oakland in 1956, and continued to practice law there for 60 years, retiring at age 86. Jim chaired the firm’s Business and Corporate Transactions and Estates & Trusts Practice Groups for many years. A respected attorney and always a gentleman, Jim served as a mentor and friend to numerous attorneys through the years. He served on the Board of Directors of the Probate and Estate Planning Section, Alameda County Bar Association (1968-1971), and was Chair of the Governing Committee of the State Bar of California Continuing Education of the Bar (CEB) (1973).
